query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic NiCoCr or CoCrFeNi) with a constant grain size, increased local chemical ordering induced by lower-temperature annealing will lead to higher hardness and yield strength (approximately 20–30% increase) relative to a high-temperature annealed, near-random solid solution, due to enhanced fluctuations in local shear‐fault energy that more effectively pin dislocations.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single-phase FCC HEA (e.g., equiatomic NiCoCr or CoCrFeNi) produced by rapid solidification, yielding a uniform random solid solution with a controlled grain size (~20 µm).
generation.intervention: Apply two different heat treatments: one set is annealed at a lower temperature (e.g., 700°C for 24 hours) to promote local chemical ordering, and the other is annealed at a higher temperature (e.g., 900°C for 24 hours) to maintain a near-random solid solution, all while preserving the grain size.
generation.conditions: All samples have identical composition and similar grain sizes (controlled via subsequent thermomechanical processing). Mechanical tests (nanoindentation, tensile/compression) are conducted at room temperature and identical strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced local chemical ordering raises the local variability of atomic bonding and shear-fault energies, resulting in a more heterogeneous lattice strain field that roughens dislocation slip pathways and creates additional effective dislocation pinning sites.
generation.mechanism: The increased LCO creates spatial fluctuations in the local shear-fault energy landscape, which imposes higher energy barriers against dislocation motion. This increased dislocation pinning leads to higher yield strength and hardness compared to a sample with a more uniform, random chemical distribution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples annealed at the lower temperature (with increased LCO) will exhibit approximately 20–30% higher hardness and yield strength compared to the high-temperature annealed baseline.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the homogenized HEA with minimal local chemical ordering (random solid solution) achieved via high-temperature annealing.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold for single-phase FCC HEAs where precipitation, grain boundary strengthening, or other mechanisms are minimized. It may not apply if processing conditions lead to phase separation or significant changes in grain size.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include precisely quantifying the degree of LCO, maintaining constant grain size during annealing, and potential confounding effects from residual stresses. Dislocation dynamics and the sensitivity of mechanical tests to LCO variations may also introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples with identical composition and controlled grain sizes. Anneal one set at 700°C for 24 hours to induce LCO and the other at 900°C for 24 hours to maintain a near-random distribution. Characterize the degree of local chemical order (via atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM) and then measure hardness (using nanoindentation) and yield strength (via tensile or compression tests).
measurements: Quantitative LCO levels from APT or TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples annealed at 700°C (with increased LCO) do not show a statistically significant increase (e.g., ≥20%) in hardness and yield strength compared to the 900°C annealed baseline, or if no correlation between increased LCO and local shear‐fault energy fluctuations is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: SignificanceComplex concentrated alloys (CCAs) with multi elements in equiatomic ratios are exotic alloys but what governs their strength is currently not clearly understood. This work has proven the prime origin of strength in CCAs as arising from the fluctuations (not the averaged value) of the shear-fault energy, which is an important feature of CCAs unrecognized beforehand. Through identification of the local hard atomic motifs far beyond the traditional concept of the globally averaged short-range ordering parameters, this work has unfolded the physical basis of strength in CCAs and provides important clues for designing high-strength CCAs by focusing on the alloy composition to produce large fault-energy fluctuations. Local chemical short-range ordering (SRO) and spatial fluctuations of planar fault energy are important features of multi-element and metastable complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). Arising from them, dislocations in such alloys are distinctively wavy in both static and migrating conditions; yet, such effects on strength have remained unknown. SignificanceWhile high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or complex concentrated alloys are touted as potential game changer alloys, many fundamental gaps remain in our understanding of these alloys. In particular, the local atomic distributions and their propensity for chemical ordering in HEAs have garnered much interest recently. Conceptually, our paper shows that systematic control of the nature and qualitative extent of ordering in HEAs is possible, starting from simple thermodynamic binary heats of mixing considerations and correlating that with corresponding mechanical properties. High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. In contrast, severe plastic deformation reduces the LCO towards random SS. Multi-principal-element alloys have been assumed to have the configurational entropy of an ideal solution. Solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, and grain boundary strengthening play different roles in determining the mechanical properties of HEAs. In most research works, solid solution strengthening caused by lattice distortion was identified to be the dominant mechanism to explain the difference in mechanical properties when an element with a large atomic radius was added to the CoCrFeNi alloy [,,,]. Precipitation strengthening is common in dual-phase HEAs, but the number of reports in the literature that explain the relationship between the volume fraction of the precipitated phase and the nanohardness of the phase to that of the macroscopic mechanical properties are relatively less [,,,]. In addition, the grain boundary strengthening mechanism was also used to explain the difference in mechanical properties by the Hall–Petch equation [,,], wherein the smaller the grain size, the higher the strength of the alloy. Therefore, the influence of grain boundary size on the mechanical properties of the alloy has been qualitatively analyzed.

SignificanceMulti–principal element alloys exhibit outstanding mechanical properties owing to severe atomic lattice distortion. However, the heterogeneous strain caused by lattice distortion at the microscopic or mesoscopic scale has been ignored for a long time because the heterogeneous strain field is difficult to quantify and characterize. Our experiments and simulations clearly show that the heterogeneous strain field can contribute to the enhanced mechanical properties of multi–principal element alloys through the new heterogeneous strain-induced strengthening mechanisms, leading to the strength-ductility synergy in severely distorted compositionally complex crystals. Multi–principal element alloys (MPEAs) exhibit outstanding mechanical properties because the core effect of severe atomic lattice distortion is distinctly different from that of traditional alloys. However, at the mesoscopic scale the underlying physics for the abundant dislocation activities responsible for strength-ductility synergy has not been uncovered. papers.title: Heterogeneous lattice strain strengthening in severely distorted crystalline solids.
papers.approach: 3D discrete dislocation dynamics simulation incorporating an experimentally measured lattice strain field
papers.findings: The study shows that the heterogeneous lattice strain field, arising from severe atomic lattice distortion, can pin dislocations and thereby enhance mechanical properties, contributing to a strength-ductility synergy that is not observed in traditional alloys.
papers.mechanism: Dislocation pinning via a heterogeneous lattice strain field produced by random mixing of multiple principal elements.

papers.title: Dislocation flow turbulence simultaneously enhances strength and ductility.
papers.approach: An atomic-lattice-distortion-dependent discrete dislocation dynamics framework combining random field theory with a phenomenological dislocation model
papers.findings: The work identifies that chemical short-range order induces higher strain peaks and wider strain wavelengths in the lattice, which in turn produces turbulent dislocation flow. This turbulence yields a unique dislocation pattern acting as both a source and trap of dislocations, enhancing both strength and ductility relative to conventional alloys.
papers.mechanism: Turbulent dislocation motion resulting from heterogeneous lattice strain linked to chemical short-range order, which modulates dislocation dynamics and yields enhanced strength.

papers.title: Strengthening in multi-principal element alloys with local-chemical-order roughened dislocation pathways.
papers.approach: Atomistic simulations (using a combination of molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo methods) to probe local chemical order (LCO) and its effect on dislocation paths
papers.findings: LCO leads to a rugged energy landscape that raises activation barriers against dislocation motion and thereby increases lattice friction. Variability in LCO explains differences in dislocation splitting, stacking fault energy, and ultimately the mechanical strength observed under different processing conditions.
papers.mechanism: Roughening of dislocation pathways via variable local chemical order, which increases the energy required for dislocation movement through nanoscale segment detrapping processes.

papers.title: Maximum strength and dislocation patterning in multi-principal element alloys.
papers.approach: Large-scale atomistic simulations examining grain-dependent dislocation structures and their evolution under uniaxial stress
papers.findings: The presence of short-range order (SRO) substantially increases maximum strength while reducing the tendency for deformation faulting. The study links differences in dislocation patterns (e.g., planar slip versus diffuse networks) with grain orientations and slip plane activities across different samples.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced dislocation resistance through increased back stress and the creation of diffuse antiphase boundaries due to SRO, which in turn delays dislocation motion.

papers.title: Fluctuations in local shear-fault energy produce unique and dominating strengthening in metastable complex concentrated alloys.
papers.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations focusing on the local fluctuations of shear-fault energy and their effect on dislocation geometry
papers.findings: The paper demonstrates that local fluctuations in shear-fault energy (as opposed to average values) dominate the strengthening response by creating variable pinning sites. This results in wavy dislocation configurations that enhance the resistance to dislocation glide.
papers.mechanism: Localized fluctuations in shear-fault energy establish hard atomic motifs that act as effective dislocation pinning centers, thereby controlling the overall yield and flow strength.

papers.title: Exceptional enhancement of mechanical properties in high-entropy alloys via thermodynamically guided local chemical ordering.
papers.approach: A combination of thermodynamic modelling (using binary heats of mixing), atom probe tomography, high-resolution electron microscopy, and density functional theory to correlate chemical ordering with mechanical performance
papers.findings: Controlled additions of alloying elements (such as Al and Ti) lead to increased local chemical order, which in turn produces a fourfold increase in tensile yield strength while also improving ductility.
papers.mechanism: Thermodynamically guided local chemical ordering modifies dislocation motion by altering the local energy landscape, thus enhancing both yield strength and ductility.

papers.title: Strengthening Mechanisms in CoCrFeNiX0.4 (Al, Nb, Ta) High Entropy Alloys Fabricated by Powder Plasma Arc Additive Manufacturing.
papers.system: CoCrFeNi-based HEAs with equal atomic radius additions (Al, Nb, Ta)
papers.approach: Experimental study employing powder plasma arc additive manufacturing, followed by detailed microstructural characterization and mechanical testing
papers.findings: The study finds that while solid solution strengthening is present, precipitation strengthening and grain boundary strengthening dominate the enhancement of mechanical properties. Notably, the HEA with Ta exhibited the best mechanical performance, attributed to the formation of a fine eutectic structure and low-angle grain boundaries.
papers.mechanism: A combined effect from solid solution, precipitation, and grain boundary strengthening with lattice distortion effects playing an indirect role in modifying dislocation dynamics.

established: High-entropy alloys exhibit enhanced hardness and strength due to a combination of mechanisms including solid solution strengthening, grain boundary effects, precipitation strengthening, and dislocation pinning from heterogeneous lattice strain.
Local chemical order and associated fluctuations in lattice properties (e.g., shear-fault energy) significantly influence dislocation behavior and hence the yield and flow strength.

Atomistic and mesoscale simulations have already demonstrated that microstructural heterogeneity in HEAs leads to non-classical dislocation dynamics, which are critical for the improved mechanical properties.

approaches_tried.approach: Discrete dislocation dynamics simulations with input from experimental lattice strain measurements
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that heterogeneous strain fields can pin dislocations effectively, enhancing both strength and ductility.

approaches_tried.approach: Atomistic simulations (MD/MC) to resolve the effects of local chemical order on fault energies and dislocation pathways
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed that local chemical order increases activation barriers for dislocation motion by creating a more rugged energy landscape, thus leading to increased mechanical strength.

mechanisms: Heterogeneous lattice strain inducing dislocation pinning
Local chemical ordering creating a rugged energy landscape and modifying planar fault energies
Fluctuations in local shear-fault energy leading to variable dislocation pinning sites
Dislocation flow turbulence generated by nonuniform lattice distortions and chemical short-range order
disagreements: The relative significance of solid solution strengthening versus precipitation and grain boundary strengthening is debated across studies.
There is ongoing discussion regarding the impact of local chemical order on mechanical properties, with some studies emphasizing its dominance and others finding its effects secondary.
Models differ in the treatment of dislocation control mechanisms (e.g., screw vs. edge dislocations) and their corresponding strengthening contributions.
open_questions: How can fluctuations in local lattice strain and shear-fault energy be quantitatively linked to yield strength and hardness in HEAs?
What is the precise, tunable role of local chemical order in governing dislocation dynamics as compared to other strengthening mechanisms?
Can a controlled experiment decouple the effects of grain boundary strengthening from lattice distortion and local ordering to pinpoint the dominant source of hardness?
opportunities: Design controlled comparisons between HEAs with deliberately varied degrees of local chemical order (through annealing or compositional adjustments) and random solid solutions.
Leverage additive manufacturing and controlled cooling techniques to decouple grain size effects from intrinsic lattice distortion mechanisms.
Conduct temperature- and strain-rate–dependent studies to further validate if local fluctuations (in shear-fault energy or lattice strain) consistently predict enhanced strengthening.
Integrate high-resolution microscopy (such as STEM with atom probe tomography) with mechanical testing to directly correlate nanoscale order features with dislocation behavior.

directions.direction: Tuning local chemical order via compositional modifications
directions.assessment: Altering the alloying elements can directly change the local bonding environments and induce variations in chemical short‐range order (LCO). Evidence indicates LCO modulates shear‐fault energy fluctuations (see PMC10041143 and PMC6687833), which is linked to dislocation pinning. This approach is fairly direct, though it may introduce secondary phases if the composition deviates too much.

directions.direction: Modifying annealing treatments to control the degree of LCO
directions.assessment: Adjusting annealing temperature and time can systematically tune the degree of local chemical ordering without altering the overall composition or grain size. Studies (e.g., PMC6687833) support that lower annealing temperatures increase LCO. This method isolates the effect of chemical order on dislocation dynamics and is both feasible and directly linked to hardness/strength.

directions.direction: Modeling and simulation of dislocation dynamics with variable LCO
directions.assessment: Using atomistic or discrete dislocation dynamics simulations allows one to explicitly assess how fluctuations in lattice strain from LCO affect dislocation pinning and yield strength. literature (e.g., PMC9231497, PMC10990144) supports this route. It is highly informative but requires experimental validation.

Techniques such as TEM combined with atom probe tomography can directly quantify local chemical ordering and correlate these measurements with dislocation structures and hardness tests. This approach is descriptive and can reveal correlations, though it may be less controlled in a comparative experiment.

directions.direction: Controlling thermomechanical processing (e.g., additive manufacturing with tailored cooling rates)
directions.assessment: Processes such as laser melting deposition (LMD) can be tuned to influence both grain structure and the degree of lattice distortion. However, decoupling the effects of grain boundaries from chemical ordering is challenging. Evidence from PMC8001620 shows multiple strengthening contributions that might confound isolating the LCO effect.

choice.direction: Modifying annealing treatments to control the degree of LCO
choice.why: This approach directly isolates the effect of local chemical order on dislocation pinning and thus on hardness and strength, while keeping the composition and grain size nearly constant. Prior work (PMC6687833) demonstrates that annealing at different temperatures modulates LCO, making it a practical and highly controlled experimental variable.
